slides.0.title: Course Introduction
slides.0.content: Bordeaux winemaking combines centuries of traditional wisdom with modern science. From the moment grapes enter the cellar, every decision shapes the final wine's quality and style. This course explores the complete red and white winemaking process—from destemming and maceration to MLF, fermentation control and maceration management—offering a comprehensive understanding of how winemaking techniques shape colour, tannin, flavour and ageing potential. You will learn how technical directors at top châteaux balance tradition and innovation to preserve terroir character while using modern technology to enhance quality consistency.

slides.1.description: Understanding the Complete Process and Key Technologies of Red Wine Winemaking
slides.2.title: Red Wine Winemaking Introduction
slides.2.content:
Red wine winemaking is a complex process transforming grapes into quality red wine. Bordeaux winemaking combines traditional wisdom and modern science; every step profoundly affects the final wine's colour, tannin structure, flavour complexity and ageing potential.

From the moment grapes enter the cellar, the winemaker must make a series of critical decisions on destemming, maceration extraction, fermentation control and pressing timing. These decisions affect not only the current vintage's quality but also the wine's ageing potential for decades to come.

Core Content of This Chapter

• Destemming

Understand the mechanical impact on grape integrity; learn to adjust the destemming ratio based on vintage character

• Maceration Extraction

Master the extraction kinetics of colour, tannin and flavour; learn the application timing of cold maceration, pump-over and punch-down

• Alcoholic Fermentation

Learn how temperature affects aroma retention and extraction efficiency; understand the impact of yeast selection on wine style

• Malolactic Fermentation

Understand how MLF softens acidity and stabilises the body, and its application strategies for different wines

• Top Château Practices

Analyse the winemaking decisions and quality philosophy of Château Latour, Château Margaux and other leading estates

Mastering this knowledge, you will understand why Bordeaux continues to produce the world's finest red wines, and how winemakers express terroir through precise technical control.
slides.3.title: Red Wine Winemaking Process Overview
slides.3.content:
Bordeaux red wine production is a precisely controlled process requiring the winemaker's professional judgement and technical execution at every step.

1️⃣ Harvest & Sorting

  • Timing: determined by sugar, acidity and phenolic maturity
  • Hand vs Machine: top châteaux mostly hand-harvested to ensure grape integrity
  • Sorting: vibrating table and optical sorter remove unhealthy or unripe grapes
  • Bordeaux Standard: classified growths typically perform 2–3 sortings

2️⃣ Crushing & Destemming

  • Destemming ratio: usually 100%, some vintages retain 5–10% of stems
  • Crushing intensity: gentle crushing to avoid pressing seeds and preventing bitterness
  • SO₂ addition: 10–30 mg/L to prevent oxidation and contamination

3️⃣ Cold Maceration

  • Temperature: 8–15°C
  • Duration: 3–7 days
  • Purpose: extract colour and fruit aromas without starting fermentation
  • Controversy: not all châteaux use it; some believe it dilutes terroir character

4️⃣ Alcoholic Fermentation

  • Temperature: 28–32°C (red wine)
  • Duration: 7–14 days
  • Yeast: natural vs commercial yeast
  • Monitored parameters: density, temperature, residual sugar, volatile acidity

5️⃣ Maceration

  • Total maceration time: 15–30 days (including fermentation period)
  • Techniques: pump-over, punch-down, rack-and-return, délestage
  • Goal: extract colour, tannin and flavour compounds

6️⃣ Pressing & Blending

  • Free-run wine: wine released before pressing (highest quality)
  • Press wine: stronger structure, higher tannin
  • Preliminary blending: decide on variety and batch mixing ratios

7️⃣ Malolactic Fermentation

  • Timing: usually starts naturally after alcoholic fermentation
  • Temperature: 18–22°C
  • Duration: 2–6 weeks
  • Effect: reduces acidity, increases smoothness, brings creamy and nutty aromas

slides.7.content:

slides.9.title: White Wine Winemaking: Fundamental Differences from Red Wine
slides.9.content:
Core philosophy: Protection over Extraction — from crisp dry white to sweet white, each has its unique winemaking logic
🛡️
Oxidation Protection
· Low phenolics, extremely prone to oxidation/browning
· Inert gas (N₂/CO₂) protection throughout
· SO₂ 50–80 mg/L (higher than red wine)
· Stricter temperature control
🌡️
Low-Temperature Fermentation
· Temperature: 16–20°C (red wine 28–32°C)
· Duration: 2–4 weeks (red wine 7–14 days)
· Purpose: retain volatile fruit aromas
🍇
Pressing First
· Press then ferment (opposite of red wine)
· Pressing intensity determines wine style
· Juice clarity affects final quality
Three Main Types of Bordeaux White Wine
🥗 Crisp Dry White
Entre-Deux-Mers style
Goal: fresh, fruity, easy-drinking
· Stainless steel 15–18°C low-temp fermentation
· Block MLF · early bottling (12–18 months)
· Aromatic yeasts
€5–15/bottle
🍾 Complex Dry White
Pessac-Léognan style
Goal: complex, structured, ageable
· Barrel fermentation (20–50% new oak)
· MLF in barrel · sur lie 6–12 months
· Delayed bottling (18–24 months)
€25–200+/bottle
🍯 Noble Rot Sweet White
Sauternes style
Goal: sweet, complex, ultra-long ageing
· Botrytis infection · 6–8 selective harvests
· Barrel fermentation (50–100% new oak)
· Residual sugar 120–150 g/L
€30–500+/bottle (375ml)

slides.15.title: Traditional Winemaking Philosophy Introduction
slides.15.content:
In an era of rapidly evolving modern technology, top Bordeaux châteaux still uphold the core tenets of traditional winemaking philosophy: minimal intervention, quality first, and preservation of technique. These principles are not conservatism but rather wisdom crystallised over centuries of validation.

Content Explored in This Chapter

🌿 Minimal Intervention Philosophy

Preserving authentic expression of grapes and terroir, avoiding over-manipulation causing stylistic homogenisation

✋ Value of Manual Operations

Understanding why premium châteaux insist on hand work, and the importance of hand selection and delicate handling

🏺 Traditional Processing Techniques

Learning natural settling, manual racking, egg white fining and other time-tested methods

⚖️ Tradition and Innovation

Exploring how to find the optimal balance between respecting tradition and embracing technology

⏳ Value of Time

Recognising the importance of patience and waiting in winemaking, understanding why one cannot rush

Understanding these traditional philosophies will help you appreciate why Bordeaux can maintain exceptional quality century after century, and how these principles continue to play a role in modern winemaking.

slides.16.content:

Minimal Intervention

slides.17.title: Traditional Clarification and Processing Methods
slides.17.content:
⏬ Natural Settling (Gravity Clarification)
Use gravity to allow impurities to naturally settle, requires patiently resting 24–48 hours. No chemical agents needed, preserves the wine's natural character.
🔄 Manual Racking (Racking)
Carefully transfer clear wine to new containers, avoiding disturbing the sediment at the bottom. Usually every 3–4 months, promotes micro-oxygenation and purification.
🥚 Protein Fining (egg white / fish glue)
Use natural fining agents to remove harsh tannins and suspended matter, traditional and effective. Classified growths typically use 2–6 egg whites per barrel.
🌿 Retaining Stems (optional)
In mature vintages retain 5–15% of stems to add structure and freshness, but must ensure maturity to avoid green/harsh notes.
📌 Traditional methods emphasise stability and integration, slower but more restrained style · Modern technology can supplement, but the core remains respect for raw materials and time
slides.18.title: The Birth of Liquid Gold
slides.18.content:
Sauternes produces the world's most complex, most expensive, longest-ageing sweet whites — dependent on a special fungus and centuries of winemaking wisdom
🍄
The Noble Rot Miracle
Under specific conditions, Botrytis cinerea penetrates grape skin without destroying the fruit, promotes water evaporation, concentrates sugars, acidity and flavour compounds, and produces unique aromatic molecules. The same fungus without drying conditions becomes destructive grey mould.
🌫️
Unique Microclimate
At the confluence of the Garonne and Ciron rivers — the cold Ciron water creates morning mist in autumn (providing humidity for noble rot), afternoon sunlight disperses fog (preventing grey mould outbreak). This "morning wet → afternoon dry" microclimate is extremely rare globally.
⏳
Long High-Risk Harvest
· Harvest period 6–10 weeks
· 6–8 selective harvests (sometimes 10+)
· Each time picking only optimally botrytised grapes
· Extremely low yield: approx. 1 glass of wine per vine
⚗️
Extremely Slow Fermentation
High sugar (300–450 g/L) creates high osmotic pressure, fermentation may last months. Alcohol rises to 13–14% then stops, leaving 120–150 g/L residual sugar. Cost is 10–20× that of regular dry white.
💰
Sky-High Price and Longevity
Top Sauternes (d'Yquem) priced at €300–1,000/375ml, still vibrant after decades to a century. Not just wine — consumable art and investment object.

slides.20.subtitle: Sauternes: The Birth of Liquid Gold
slides.20.description: Exploring the Winemaking Secrets of the World's Finest Sweet White Wine
slides.21.title: Sweet Wine Production and Noble Rot Science Introduction
slides.21.content:
The sweet white wines of Sauternes and Barsac represent the pinnacle of winemaking. The creation of this "liquid gold" depends on the miraculous transformation by noble rot, unique microclimate conditions, and the extreme patience and skill of the winemaker.

Unlike ordinary wines, Sauternes production is full of risk and challenge. From waiting for botrytis infection to multiple selective harvests, from the extremely slow fermentation to years of barrel ageing, every stage requires the winemaker's professional judgement and persistence. Costs are 10–20× ordinary dry white, but in return comes legendary wine capable of ageing for a century.

In-Depth Analysis of This Chapter

🍄 Biological Mechanism of Noble Rot

Understand how Botrytis cinerea transforms grapes, master the key differences between noble rot and grey mould, and the required environmental conditions

🌫️ Unique Microclimate Conditions

Recognise the unique fog environment of Sauternes, understand how the confluence of the Garonne and Ciron rivers creates ideal conditions

🍇 Strategy and Challenges of Selective Harvesting

Learn why 6–10 (or more) harvests are needed, understand how to assess optimal botrytis level, grasp economic and technical considerations

⚗️ Technical Challenges of High-Sugar Fermentation

Master the management of extremely slow fermentation (4–8 months), understand the impact of high osmotic pressure on yeast, learn how to balance sweetness and alcohol level

👑 Château d'Yquem Ultimate Quality Model

Analyse the winemaking decisions of the world's finest sweet wine, understand the "quality over quantity" philosophy, explore investment value and market positioning

Studying this chapter, you will understand why Sauternes can remain vibrant after a century of ageing, and why this "liquid gold" is so precious. This is not merely wine but an artwork co-created by the winemaker and nature.
slides.22.title: Sauternes Winemaking Process: Six Stages of Extreme Precision
slides.23.title: Case Study: Château d'Yquem's Ultimate Quality Model
slides.23.content:
Core Challenge
How to consistently produce top sweet whites with 50–100 year ageing potential under high-risk climate and extreme costs?
🛠 Key Practices + Cost Thinking
· Multiple (6–8+) selective harvests ensure botrytis uniformity
· All-new barrels long maturation + no MLF to retain acid tension
· Strict batch sensory + chemical dual screening
· No production in poor vintages (e.g. 2012 no grand vin)
· Second label (dry white) flexibly absorbs batches not meeting grand vin standard
💰 Cost Structure
· Yield only ~⅓ of AOC limit (≈9 hL/ha vs 25 hL/ha)
· Approx. 1 glass of wine per vine
· Long-term brand capital > short-term cash flow
🏆 Quality Outcomes + Market Position
· Sensory: rich layers + elongated acid backbone + silky viscosity
· Ageing: 50–100 years (great vintages >150 years still vibrant)
· Current vintages €300–400, great vintages €500–800, historic vintages auction €10K+
🍯 Flavour Signature
Honey · apricot · mango · candied citrus · caramel
Saffron · spices · beeswax notes
Acidity support makes sweet without cloying, lingering finish
💡 Key Learnings
Moat Thinking
Extreme standards + rejection rate is core guarantee of brand capital
New Barrel Prerequisite
High new barrel ratio requires sufficient raw material concentration to support, otherwise counterproductive
Quality over Quantity
Not producing in poor vintage years yields far greater long-term brand returns than short-term cash flow loss
Human-Machine Collaboration
Optical sorting technology assists rather than replaces guided manual judgement
slides.24.title: Knowledge Check: Sweet Wine Production and Noble Rot
slides.25.title: Sweet Wine Production: The Ultimate Balance of Risk and Reward
slides.25.content:
**Core Insights:**

🍄 **Dual Nature of Noble Rot**: same fungus, different manifestations; requires a "morning wet + afternoon dry" microclimate window.
🛠 **Harvest Strategy**: 6–8 selective harvests amplify labour costs but raise the quality ceiling.
⚗️ **High-Sugar Fermentation Management**: stress-tolerant yeast cultivation, control volatile acidity, avoid reduction and stuck fermentation.
🪵 **Oak and Time**: new barrels and extended barrel ageing assist redox buffering, integrating high concentrations of sugar/acid/flavour molecules.
💰 **Economic Structure**: low yield + high labour intensity + high ageing potential = collectible and investment attributes.
🌍 **Future Challenges**: climate change eroding stability → requires more precise data/selection technology (optical sorting, AI assessment).

slides.28.title: Oak Barrels: The Soul Companion of Winemaking
slides.28.content: Oak barrels serve multiple roles as container, flavour agent, micro-oxygenator and structure modifier — a dynamic chemical/physical/microbial reactor. Their influence comes from: chemical extraction (vanillin, lactones, eugenol, furfural, oak tannins), slow micro-oxygenation (promoting anthocyanin stabilisation and tannin polymerisation), and interaction with lees/microorganisms (texture and reductive protection).

slides.30.title: Oak Barrel Science Fundamentals
slides.30.subtitle: The Science from Forest to Cellar
slides.30.description: Understanding How Oak Shapes Wine Flavour and Structure
slides.31.title: Oak Barrel Science Fundamentals Introduction
slides.31.content:
Oak barrels are dynamic chemical and biological reactors — chemical extraction, slow micro-oxygenation, and lees interaction: three layers of mechanism shaping wine style.

A quality oak barrel's influence comes from three dimensions: chemical extraction (vanillin, lactones, eugenol, oak tannins), slow micro-oxygenation (promoting anthocyanin stability and tannin polymerisation), and interaction with lees (enhancing texture and complexity). Understanding these scientific principles is key to evaluating wine quality and style.

Key Learning Points of This Chapter

🌳 Differences in Oak Species

European oak (Quercus robur / sessilis) vs American oak (Quercus alba) — grain tightness determines extraction rate and aroma profile

🇫🇷 French Region Characteristics

Tronçais / Allier / Limousin / Vosges / Nevers — density, tannin and vanillin differences, precise matching to wine objectives

🔬 Chemical Composition Analysis

Vanillin / lactones / eugenol / furfural — how different compounds are released and their impact on aroma and structure

📊 Extraction Kinetics

First 6–12 months extraction fastest, followed by gradual deceleration — understanding time curve to optimise ageing strategy

⚖️ New/Used Barrel Strategy

How to configure new barrel ratio; decision logic and risk-reward for top château barrel ageing strategies
slides.32.title: Oak Species: The Origin of Flavour
slides.32.content:
Core classification: European Oak vs American Oak — grain tightness determines extraction rate and aroma profile
🇪🇺 European Oak
Quercus robur / sessilis
Structure: tight growth rings, small vessels
Extraction: slow release, elegant and gradual
Aroma: refined spice, mineral
Tannin: strong structure, good antioxidant capacity
Vanillin 1–5 mg/L ｜ Lactones 1–3 mg/L
🇺🇸 American Oak
Quercus alba
Structure: loose growth rings, larger vessels
Extraction: fast, intense one-off impact
Aroma: vanilla, coconut, pronounced sweetness
Tannin: lower, smoother mouthfeel
Vanillin 5–15 mg/L ｜ Lactones 3–10 mg/L
🔬 Anatomical Differences and Impact
Vessel size / growth ring tightness / density → determines extraction rate and micro-oxygenation rhythm. Tight (Tronçais) = elegant gradual; Loose (Limousin) = intense rapid.
💡 Winemaking Impact
Tight grain = slow release; loose grain = fast release + stronger one-off impact. Bordeaux top red wines primarily use European oak, pursuing refined gradual flavour integration.

slides.34.title: Oak Barrel Manufacturing Craft
slides.34.subtitle: The Art of Air-Drying and Toasting
slides.34.description: Exploring the Traditional Craft of Top-Tier Cooperages
slides.35.title: Oak Barrel Manufacturing Craft Introduction
slides.35.content:
Creating a top oak barrel requires years — from selection and air-drying to toasting, every stage is an investment in flavour.

Cooperage is not only technique but also art. From selecting 150–200 year-old oaks, to 24–60 months of natural air-drying, then precisely controlled toasting, every stage affects the final flavour expression. This is why top new oak barrels can cost €800–1,200, and their influence can last 3–5 years.

In-Depth Content of This Chapter

🌬️ Natural Air-Drying: Time and Chemical Changes

24–60 months of natural drying softens tannins, releases aroma precursors — cannot be replaced by kiln drying

🔥 Toasting Science and Temperature Control

160–220°C pyrolysis, Maillard reaction and caramelisation — multi-layer reactions building the flavour profile

🎯 Flavour Characteristics of Toast Levels

Light: fresh coconut → Medium: vanilla/nuts → Medium-Plus: caramel/coffee → Heavy: coffee/smoke

🏭 Custom Services of Top Cooperages

Taransaud / Seguin Moreau — material selection, drying cycles and custom toasting programme craft heritage

💰 Oak Barrel Quality Assessment

Top new barrels €800–1,200, influence lasting 3–5 years; understand cost-benefit logic and ROI thinking
slides.36.title: Air-Drying: The Catalyst of Time
slides.36.content:
Air-drying 24–60 months: water evaporation → chemical transformation → aroma precursor release — time is the cost of complexity
🌬️ Ideal Air-Drying Conditions
· Temperature 15–25°C (avoid extremes)
· Humidity 60–80% RH (microbial action)
· Ventilation: avoid standing water and rot
· Avoid direct rain: prevent excessive bitterness leaching
· Slats spaced + regular turning for uniform drying
· Top cooperages have outdoor yards spanning several hectares managing tens of thousands of staves
⏱️ Natural vs Kiln Drying
⚡ Kiln Dry
2–4 weeks
Dehydration only
Low cost
Bitterness unsoftened, aroma precursors not accumulated
✅ Air Dry
24–60 months
Complete chemical maturation
Tannin hydrolysis + lactone precursor accumulation + bitterness softening
Top cooperages insist on the long natural process
⚠️ Too short (<18 months) = harsh green tannins; too long (>60 months) = excessive capital tied up, diminishing returns. Golden zone: Bordeaux top cooperage standard 36 months (Tronçais often 60 months).

slides.46.title: Modern Sorting Technology
slides.46.subtitle: Evolution from Manual to AI
slides.46.description: How Technology Enhances Grape Quality Control
slides.47.title: Modern Sorting Technology Introduction
slides.47.content:
Raw material quality is the first critical checkpoint determining wine quality. Modern sorting technology has evolved from traditional hand selection to optical sorting, X-ray detection, even AI image recognition, greatly improving screening efficiency and precision.

One poor-quality grape can ruin a whole barrel of wine. Traditional hand sorting is thorough but slow (100 kg/person/hour) and prone to fatigue. Modern optical sorting can handle 3–8 tonnes/hour with 95–97% accuracy, allowing top châteaux to greatly improve efficiency while maintaining quality control. Investment is high (€200K–1.5M), but the contribution to quality improvement is immeasurable.

Topics Explored in This Chapter

🔍 Optical Sorting Principles and Advantages

Multi-spectral analysis + high-speed camera, 3–8 t/h — understanding how optical sorting achieves 95–97% accuracy

⚙️ X-Ray Internal Defect Detection

97–99% accuracy, suitable for top-grade selection — precise identification of internal defects invisible to optical methods

🧠 AI Deep Learning Applications

Continuously optimises sorting standards, builds plot/vintage fingerprint database — how machine learning improves over time

📊 ROI Analysis

Capital expenditure €0 to €1.5M — understanding cost-benefit decision logic at different production scales

🏆 Château Margaux Upgrade Case Study

+300% processing efficiency — how systematic technology deployment transforms raw material quality control

Learning these technologies, you will understand how modern châteaux ensure raw material consistency while using technology to improve efficiency without losing precision quality control. This is a model example of perfect combination of traditional craft and modern technology.

slides.51.title: Precision Fermentation Control System
slides.51.subtitle: From Experience to Data-Driven
slides.51.description: Modern Fermentation Monitoring and Automation Technology
slides.52.title: Precision Fermentation Control Introduction
slides.52.content:
Fermentation is the most critical stage of winemaking. Modern fermentation control technology combines traditional empirical judgement with precision sensors and automation systems, achieving unprecedented stability and reproducibility.

A 1°C temperature difference can change aroma retention and extraction efficiency; fermentation stalling can cause an entire barrel to be discarded. Modern systems achieve ±0.1°C precision control through multi-point PT100 sensors, combined with PID predictive models for automatic adjustment, elevating the fermentation process from "art" to "controllable science". This does not replace the winemaker's experience, but allows experience to be precisely executed.

Core Content of This Chapter

🌡️ Precision Temperature Monitoring System

Multi-point PT100 sensors ±0.1°C, jacket and internal cooling coil coordination, predictive curves to avoid temperature peaks

📊 Real-Time Fermentation Kinetics Tracking

Online densimeter monitors density/sugar changes, precision ±0.001, 48-hour no-drop stall warning

🔄 Programmable Automatic Pump-Over System

Frequency/intensity/timing window settings, reduce human variation, strengthen reproducibility across batches and vintages

🧪 PID Control and Predictive Models

Proportional-integral-derivative control for precise adjustment, predictive model to pre-empt fermentation changes before they occur

🔄 Rotary Fermentation Tank Innovation

Improves skin contact efficiency, shortens maceration cycle, only for high-value batches — cost-benefit considerations

Mastering these technologies, you will understand how modern châteaux precisely control the fermentation process, improving quality stability while maintaining traditional style. This is best practice in data-driven winemaking.

slides.55.title: Post-Processing Technology Innovation
slides.55.subtitle: Clarification, Stabilisation and Concentration
slides.55.description: How Modern Technology Enhances Wine Quality
slides.56.title: Post-Processing Technology Innovation Introduction
slides.56.content:
The post-processing stage after fermentation is equally important. Modern technologies such as membrane filtration, reverse osmosis and freeze concentration provide winemakers with more options, but how to apply these technologies while preserving terroir character remains an art.

Post-processing technology is a double-edged sword. Membrane filtration can improve stability and preserve flavour, but while reverse osmosis concentration can boost concentration it may alter authentic terroir expression. 60% of Bordeaux châteaux use membrane filtration, but only 30% occasionally use RO, and 5% experiment with freeze concentration. Technology selection is not only a scientific decision but involves winemaking philosophy, regulatory constraints and ethical boundaries.

Key Learning Points of This Chapter

🧪 Membrane Filtration Technology Family

Cross-flow, UF, MF, NF principles and applications, reducing wine loss 1–2% and chemical agent dependence

🔄 Controversy of Reverse Osmosis Concentration

RO technology at 30–80 bar, +2% vol regulatory limit, "altering composition ratios" terroir authenticity debate

❄️ Advantages and Challenges of Freeze Concentration

Low-temperature physical separation for high aroma retention, high energy consumption €0.30–0.80/L, wine loss 10–25%

📊 Quality Impact of Different Technologies

Membrane filtration positive stabilising, RO concentration boost but aroma loss risk, freeze high retention but extreme cost

⚖️ Regulatory Limits and Ethical Boundaries

EU and AOC regulations, "technology tool vs terroir expression" philosophical debate — where to draw the line

After completing this chapter, you will be able to view traditional and modern technology choices in a balanced way, understand why some technologies are widely accepted while others remain controversial, and how to find the balance between technological progress and terroir respect.
